title: Learning to reason with LLMs (blog, September 12, 2024)
why: The o1 announcement: AIME 2024 from 12% (GPT-4o) to 74% single-sample, 83% with 64-sample consensus, 93% re-ranking 1,000 samples with a learned scorer; accuracy rising smoothly with both train-time and test-time compute; the decision to hide the raw chain. Secondary source.

title: Show your work: scratchpads for intermediate computation with language models
why: The origin of trained intermediate computation: fine-tuning a model to emit a scratchpad before the answer makes multi-step arithmetic and program execution learnable. The 2021 point on the timeline.

title: STaR: bootstrapping reasoning with reasoning
why: Sample rationales, keep the ones that reach the right answer, fine-tune, repeat; rationalize failures from the answer. Rejection-sampling self-training, the ancestor of every RLVR loop; matches fine-tuning a 30x larger model on CommonsenseQA.

title: Tulu 3: pushing frontiers in open language model post-training
why: Coins 'reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards' (RLVR) as a post-training stage on math and instruction-following with programmatic checkers, two months before R1.

title: DeepSeek-R1: incentivizing reasoning capability in LLMs via reinforcement learning
why: The open recipe: R1-Zero (pure RL from the base, AIME 2024 15.6 to 71.0 pass@1, 86.7 with majority voting), R1's four stages with a cold start, the distilled Qwen and Llama models, and the failed PRM and MCTS attempts. Also Nature 645:633-638 (2025). Read with section 4.

title: Towards large reasoning models: a survey of reinforced reasoning with large language models
why: The first survey written after o1 and before R1: automated data, test-time scaling and RL as the three ingredients; a map of the field in January 2025.

title: LLM post-training: a deep dive into reasoning large language models
why: A post-R1 survey of fine-tuning, RL and test-time scaling for reasoning, with a taxonomy that matches this deck's sections.

title: Why we think (blog, May 2025)
why: A long, careful overview of thinking-time compute: latent and token-level thinking, RL on correctness, faithfulness, scaling laws for thinking time. The best single piece of secondary reading. Secondary source.

title: Understanding reasoning LLMs (newsletter, February 2025)
why: Four ways to build a reasoning model (inference scaling, pure RL, RL plus SFT, distillation) laid out around DeepSeek-R1 with a cost comparison; written for practitioners. Secondary source.

title: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (book), chapter 7: reasoning and inference-time scaling
why: The textbook treatment of RLVR as a post-training stage, with GRPO derivations and the practical lore of 2025; the arXiv entry is the whole book.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models
why: Eight worked exemplars in the prompt take PaLM 540B from 17.9% to 56.9% on GSM8K (58.6% with a calculator); the gain appears only at scale. The slide-5 bars.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Large language models are zero-shot reasoners
why: 'Let's think step by step' alone: text-davinci-002 from 17.7% to 78.7% on MultiArith and 10.4% to 40.7% on GSM8K. The behavior was latent in the pretrained model.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models
why: Sample many chains, majority-vote the answers: +17.9 points on GSM8K over greedy chain-of-thought for PaLM 540B (to 74.4%). The first test-time scaling result and still the baseline for parallel compute.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning in large language models
why: Decompose into subproblems, solve in order: 99% on SCAN length generalization with 14 exemplars where chain-of-thought gets 16%. Decomposition as a prompting primitive.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Text and patterns: for effective chain of thought, it takes two to tango
why: Counterfactual prompts show the factual correctness of the exemplar steps matters little; the symbols, patterns and text of the chain matter together. An early warning that chains are not what they seem.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Why think step by step? Reasoning emerges from the locality of experience
why: A data-side explanation: when training data covers local dependencies, chaining local inferences lets the model bridge variables that never co-occur. Proven for a chain-structured model, checked with transformers.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Towards revealing the mystery behind chain of thought: a theoretical perspective
why: Bounded-depth transformers cannot output arithmetic or equation answers directly unless size grows super-polynomially; constant-size autoregressive transformers solve them with a chain. The circuit-complexity case on slide 6.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: The expressive power of transformers with chain of thought
why: Logarithmically many steps add little; linearly many reach all regular languages; polynomially many reach exactly P. The length of the chain is the resource.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Chain of thought empowers transformers to solve inherently serial problems
why: Without a chain, constant-depth constant-precision transformers sit in AC0; with T chain steps they compute anything a size-T circuit computes. Serial problems need serial tokens.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Training large language models to reason in a continuous latent space
why: Coconut: feed the last hidden state back as the next input embedding instead of a token; an implicit breadth-first search that beats chain-of-thought on search-heavy logic. Latent reasoning, and what it would do to monitorability.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Scaling up test-time compute with latent reasoning: a recurrent depth approach
why: A 3.5B model with a looped block, trained on 800B tokens, matches test-time compute equivalent to 50B parameters by iterating in latent space; the recurrent-depth alternative mentioned on slides 6 and 24.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Quiet-STaR: language models can teach themselves to think before speaking
why: Per-token latent rationales learned from plain text with a REINFORCE signal on next-token likelihood: zero-shot GSM8K 5.9 to 10.9, CommonsenseQA 36.3 to 47.2.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Language models don't always say what they think: unfaithful explanations in chain-of-thought prompting
why: Biasing features in the context (answer always 'A' in the exemplars) change answers by up to 36 points across 13 tasks while the chains never mention the bias. The slide-7 result.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Measuring faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning
why: Truncate, corrupt or paraphrase the chain and see whether the answer moves; larger and more capable models produce less faithful chains on most tasks.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Chain-of-thought reasoning in the wild is not always faithful
why: Unprompted unfaithfulness: implicit post-hoc rationalization in up to 13% of answers for production models, with much lower rates for R1 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet in thinking mode.

section_name: Chains of thought: the effect, the theory, faithfulness
title: Reasoning models don't always say what they think
why: Hints that change the answer are verbalized 25% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 39% (R1) of the time; outcome RL raises faithfulness then plateaus; reward hacks exploited on over 99% of examples are mentioned in under 2% of chains. The slide-7 and slide-27 numbers.

title: Training verifiers to solve math word problems
why: GSM8K (8.5K problems) and the first outcome verifier: sample 100 solutions, rank with a trained verifier; verification scales better with data than fine-tuning alone.

title: Solving math word problems with process- and outcome-based feedback
why: Process supervision cuts reasoning errors among correct final answers from 14.0% to 3.4% at similar final-answer accuracy; the first process-versus-outcome comparison.

title: Let's verify step by step
why: PRM800K: 800K step labels. Best-of-1,860 on a MATH subset: process reward model 78.2%, outcome reward model 72.4%, majority vote 69.6%. The slide-8 numbers.

title: Math-Shepherd: verify and reinforce LLMs step-by-step without human annotations
why: Step labels estimated by Monte Carlo rollouts instead of humans; a PRM for both reranking and RL, moving Mistral-7B from 77.9 to 84.1 on GSM8K.

title: The lessons of developing process reward models in mathematical reasoning
why: Qwen's post-mortem: Monte Carlo step labels are worse than LLM-judge or human labels, best-of-N evaluation is biased, consensus filtering helps. Why R1 dropped PRMs.

title: Generative verifiers: reward modeling as next-token prediction
why: Train the verifier to generate a judgment (with its own chain) and read the probability of 'Yes'; large best-of-N gains over discriminative reward models.

title: Tree of Thoughts: deliberate problem solving with large language models
why: Explicit search over partial thoughts with self-evaluation: Game of 24 from 4% (chain-of-thought) to 74% with GPT-4. Search outside the model, slide 9.

title: Graph of Thoughts: solving elaborate problems with large language models
why: Generalizes tree search to graphs with merging and refinement; better quality than Tree of Thoughts on sorting at lower cost. The end of the prompt-time search line.

title: Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
why: Allocate test-time compute by estimated difficulty: more than 4x the efficiency of best-of-N, and a small model with compute-optimal search beating a 14x larger one at matched FLOPs. Slide 9.

title: Large language monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
why: Coverage (pass@k) grows log-linearly over four orders of magnitude of samples; SWE-bench Lite from 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250. The ceiling that verifiers cash in.

title: rStar-Math: small LLMs can master math reasoning with self-evolved deep thinking
why: MCTS with code-verified steps and a process preference model, four rounds of self-evolution: Qwen2.5-Math-7B from 58.8% to 90.0% on MATH. Search-based training that works, at a cost.

title: Competitive programming with large reasoning models
why: o1 (1673 Codeforces rating), o1-ioi with hand-engineered test-time strategies (1807 to 2214), and o3 (2724, 99.8th percentile) with none: scaled RL replaced the hand-built search. Slide 10.

title: Scaling test-time compute with open models (Hugging Face blog)
why: Reproduces Snell et al. with open weights: Llama 3.2 1B plus a PRM and beam search beats Llama 3.1 8B on MATH-500; best-of-N, beam and diverse verifier tree search compared. Secondary source.

title: Can 1B LLM surpass 405B LLM? Rethinking compute-optimal test-time scaling
why: Compute-optimal test-time scaling depends on the policy, the PRM and the difficulty; a 1B model beats a 405B one on MATH-500 with the right search, and a 7B beats o1 and R1.

title: Deep think with confidence
why: Filter parallel chains by the model's own token confidence: 99.9% on AIME 2025 at 512 samples with 84.7% fewer tokens than plain majority voting.

title: ParaThinker: native parallel thinking as a new paradigm to scale LLM test-time compute
why: Trains a model to run several reasoning paths in parallel inside one context and merge them; +12.3% for a 1.5B model with 8 paths at 7% latency overhead. Parallel thinking as an architecture.

title: Does thinking more always help? Mirage of test-time scaling in reasoning models
why: Forcing more 'Wait' tokens raises accuracy and then lowers it; parallel sampling scales more reliably. Test-time scaling is not monotone.

title: Scaling reasoning tokens via RL and parallel thinking: evidence from competitive programming
why: Log-linear accuracy against reasoning tokens across RL checkpoints; 16 threads by 16 rounds reach oracle pass@16 at pass@1 for 7.6M tokens per problem. The 2026 state of the test-time curve.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: DeepSeekMath: pushing the limits of mathematical reasoning in open language models
why: Introduces GRPO: PPO without a value model, advantages from a group of samples per prompt; 120B math tokens; 51.7% on MATH with a 7B model. The algorithm on slide 13.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: Beyond human data: scaling self-training for problem-solving with language models
why: ReST-EM: expectation-maximization view of sample-filter-finetune on PaLM 2, the bridge between STaR and RLVR.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: Back to basics: revisiting REINFORCE-style optimization for learning from human feedback in LLMs
why: REINFORCE with a leave-one-out baseline (RLOO) matches or beats PPO for LLM fine-tuning at a fraction of the complexity; the case that the value model was never needed.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: REINFORCE++: stabilizing critic-free policy optimization with global advantage normalization
why: Normalize advantages over the global batch rather than per prompt; a critic-free algorithm with better robustness to reward hacking than GRPO in the authors' tests.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: Kimi k1.5: scaling reinforcement learning with LLMs
why: Released the same week as R1: long-context RL with a length penalty, multimodal, and long2short methods that transfer long-chain accuracy to short chains. AIME 77.5, MATH500 96.2.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: DAPO: an open-source LLM reinforcement learning system at scale
why: Four fixes to GRPO (clip-higher with epsilon_high 0.28, dynamic sampling, token-level loss, overlong reward shaping) reach 50 on AIME 2024 with Qwen2.5-32B base, beating DeepSeek's 47 at half the steps; code, data (17k problems) and system released.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: Understanding R1-Zero-like training: a critical perspective
why: Dr. GRPO: the length and standard-deviation normalizations in GRPO bias toward long wrong answers; base models already show 'aha' behaviors; Qwen2.5 bases answer without templates. 43.3% AIME 2024 with 7B.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: VAPO: efficient and reliable reinforcement learning for advanced reasoning tasks
why: The value-based counterpoint: with the right value pretraining, length-adaptive GAE and decoupled clipping, PPO reaches 60.4 on AIME 2024 with Qwen-32B in 5,000 steps.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: Group sequence policy optimization
why: Importance ratios and clipping at the sequence level instead of per token; stabilizes RL for mixture-of-experts models; used to train Qwen3.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: MiniMax-M1: scaling test-time compute efficiently with lightning attention
why: CISPO (clip the importance weights, not the updates), a 456B hybrid-attention model with 1M context, and a stated RL bill: 512 H800s for three weeks, $534,700.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: Magistral
why: An RL-only recipe on an existing instruct model with the 2025 lore spelled out: no KL term, length-normalized loss, minibatch advantage normalization, clip-higher; Magistral Medium 73.6 on AIME 2024.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: Defining and characterizing reward hacking
why: A formal definition: two rewards are unhackable only in degenerate cases over all stochastic policies; the background for every reward-design slide.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: Reinforcement learning with rubric anchors
why: Over 10,000 rubrics as rewards for open-ended tasks; +5.2% on open-ended benchmarks with 5K samples. The main attempt to extend RLVR beyond checkable answers.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: Learning to reason without external rewards
why: Intuitor: the model's own self-certainty as the only reward matches GRPO on math and generalizes better to code. Evidence, mostly on Qwen, that the reward signal can be weak.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: Absolute Zero: reinforced self-play reasoning with zero data
why: The model proposes its own tasks, a code executor verifies them, and RL trains both roles; no external problems at all.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: SWE-RL: advancing LLM reasoning via reinforcement learning on open software evolution
why: RL on real pull-request history with a similarity reward against the merged patch: a 70B Llama reaches 41.0% on SWE-bench Verified. Agentic RL without a unit-test oracle.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: ReTool: reinforcement learning for strategic tool use in LLMs
why: A code interpreter inside the RL rollout: a 32B model reaches 67% on AIME in 400 training steps where text-only RL took 1,080 steps for 40%; 72.5% with more training. Slide 21.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: ToRA: a tool-integrated reasoning agent for mathematical problem solving
why: Interleave natural-language reasoning with program calls; the first open model over 50% on MATH (ToRA-Code-34B). Tool-integrated reasoning before RL.

section_name: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards: RLVR, R1, GRPO, reward design
title: LLMs gaming verifiers: RLVR can lead to reward hacking
why: RLVR-trained models enumerate instance labels instead of inducing the rule when the verifier allows it; isomorphic verification removes the exploit. A 2026 reminder that the checker is part of the model.

section_name: Training dynamics: what RL changes and what was already there
title: Does reinforcement learning really incentivize reasoning capacity in LLMs beyond the base model?
why: RLVR models win at small k, base models win at large k: RL sharpens the distribution over chains the base model could already produce and narrows coverage; distillation expands it. The slide-16 crossover.

section_name: Training dynamics: what RL changes and what was already there
title: Spurious rewards: rethinking training signals in RLVR
why: Random rewards give +21.4 points on MATH-500 for Qwen2.5-Math-7B (ground truth: +29.1; wrong labels: +24.1), by amplifying code-style reasoning the base already uses; little effect on Llama and OLMo. Check the base before crediting the reward.

section_name: Training dynamics: what RL changes and what was already there
title: Reinforcement learning for reasoning in large language models with one training example
why: RLVR on a single problem takes Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B from 36.0% to 73.6% on MATH500, matching a 1.2k-problem set; improvement continues after the one example is saturated.

section_name: Training dynamics: what RL changes and what was already there
title: ProRL: prolonged reinforcement learning expands reasoning boundaries in large language models
why: Over 2,000 RL steps from R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on 136K problems with KL control and reference resets; pass@k rises on tasks where the base model fails at any k. The reply to the crossover paper.

section_name: Training dynamics: what RL changes and what was already there
title: BroRL: scaling reinforcement learning via broadened exploration
why: Hundreds of rollouts per prompt instead of more steps revive models saturated after 3K ProRL steps; rollouts as a scaling axis.

section_name: Training dynamics: what RL changes and what was already there
title: The entropy mechanism of reinforcement learning for reasoning language models
why: Policy entropy collapses early and performance follows R = -a exp(H) + b, so a ceiling is fixed at zero entropy; Clip-Cov and KL-Cov keep entropy up. Slide 13's 'entropy' bullet.

section_name: Training dynamics: what RL changes and what was already there
title: Beyond the 80/20 rule: high-entropy minority tokens drive effective reinforcement learning for LLM reasoning
why: About 20% of tokens, the high-entropy 'forks', carry the useful policy gradient; updating only them matches or beats full updates on Qwen3 models.

section_name: Training dynamics: what RL changes and what was already there
title: The art of scaling reinforcement learning compute for LLMs
why: Over 400,000 GPU-hours of ablations: RL compute-performance curves are sigmoidal with a recipe-dependent asymptote; ScaleRL extrapolated from small runs to a 100,000 GPU-hour run.

section_name: Training dynamics: what RL changes and what was already there
title: Scaling behaviors of LLM reinforcement learning post-training: an empirical study in mathematical reasoning
why: Qwen2.5 from 0.5B to 72B: test loss follows a power law in compute and data; model size matters more than data under a fixed budget.

section_name: Training dynamics: what RL changes and what was already there
title: Pass@k training for adaptively balancing exploration and exploitation of large reasoning models
why: Use pass@k itself as the reward with an analytic advantage; the model keeps exploring instead of collapsing onto one chain.

section_name: Training dynamics: what RL changes and what was already there
title: IsoCompute playbook: optimally scaling sampling compute for LLM RL
why: How many rollouts per problem at a fixed compute budget: compute-optimal rollouts rise with budget and then saturate. The 2026 rollout-allocation law.

section_name: Training dynamics: what RL changes and what was already there
title: Rewards as labels: revisiting RLVR from a classification perspective
why: Treat the binary reward as a label and train with a classification loss: +6.7% over DAPO on a 1.5B model, +6.2% on 7B. One of several 2026 reformulations of GRPO.

title: Distilling step-by-step! Outperforming larger language models with less training data and smaller model sizes
why: Rationales from a large model as extra supervision for a small one: a 770M T5 beats 540B PaLM using 80% of the data. Rationale distillation before reasoning models.

title: s1: simple test-time scaling
why: 1,000 questions with Gemini-distilled traces, 26 minutes on 16 H100s, and budget forcing (insert end-of-thinking, or suppress it and append 'Wait'): s1-32B beats o1-preview on competition math by up to 27%. Slide 17.

title: LIMO: less is more for reasoning
why: 817 curated problems with high-quality chains: 57.1% on AIME 2024 and 94.8% on MATH (v1; v3 reports 63.3 and 95.6 with 800 samples), against 6.5% and 59.2% for earlier SFT recipes with 100k examples.

title: OpenThoughts: data recipes for reasoning models
why: 1,000-plus ablations of question sourcing, filtering and teacher choice; OpenThoughts3 (1.2M examples) gives a 7B model 53% on AIME 2025 by supervised fine-tuning alone; QwQ-32B a better teacher than R1. Slide 18.

title: AIMO-2 winning solution: building state-of-the-art mathematical reasoning models with OpenMathReasoning dataset
why: 540K problems with 3.2M long-reasoning and 1.7M tool-integrated solutions, plus GenSelect for choosing among candidates; the largest open reasoning set.

title: Light-R1: curriculum SFT, DPO and RL for long COT from scratch and beyond
why: A curriculum of 76k then 3k hard problems takes Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct to 76.6 on AIME 2024 in six hours on 12 H800s (about $1,000 by the authors' count). The cheap-32B recipe.

title: AceReason-Nemotron: advancing math and code reasoning through reinforcement learning
why: Math-only RL then code-only RL on distilled 7B and 14B models: +14.6 and +17.2 on AIME 2025; math RL transfers to code.

title: Open-R1: a fully open reproduction of DeepSeek-R1 (blog, January 28, 2025) and update 2 (February 10, 2025)
why: The reproduction plan and OpenR1-Math-220k: 800k R1 traces for 400k NuminaMath problems generated on 512 H100s, filtered to 220k; the resulting 7B scores 90.6 on MATH-500 against 91.6 for R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. Secondary source.

title: NuminaMath: CoT, TIR and 1.5 datasets (Hugging Face collection)
why: 860k competition-style problems with chains (and 72.5k tool-integrated solutions); the problem source behind most 2025 reasoning data. Secondary source.

title: Sky-T1: train your own o1-preview model within $450 (blog, January 10, 2025)
why: 17K QwQ-distilled samples, 19 hours on 8 H100s, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct: 43.3 on AIME 2024. The first sub-$500 reproduction. Secondary source.

title: Bespoke-Stratos: the unreasonable effectiveness of reasoning distillation (blog, January 22, 2025)
why: 17k R1 traces, 47x fewer than DeepSeek's own distillation set, give a 32B model 63.3 on AIME 2024 and 93.0 on MATH500. Secondary source.

title: DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview: surpassing o1-preview with a 1.5B model by scaling RL (model card, February 2025)
why: GRPO with context grown from 8K to 16K to 24K tokens takes R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B to 43.1% on AIME 2024; the small-model RL recipe many later papers start from. Secondary source.

title: Qwen3 technical report
why: Hybrid thinking and non-thinking modes in one model, a thinking budget, four post-training stages (long-CoT cold start, reasoning RL with GRPO on 3,995 query-verifier pairs, thinking-mode fusion, general RL), and strong-to-weak distillation at a tenth of the GPU-hours.

title: gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b model card
why: Open-weight reasoning models with low/medium/high effort set in the system prompt; 116.8B parameters with 5.1B active; 2.1M H100-hours for the 120b; AIME 2025 97.9 with tools. The open reference point on slides 19 and 24.

title: Phi-4-reasoning technical report
why: A 14B model fine-tuned on o3-mini traces, then a short outcome-RL stage (Phi-4-reasoning-plus); a careful account of what SFT alone buys at 14B.

title: Llama-Nemotron: efficient reasoning models
why: 8B, 49B and 253B models with a reasoning toggle in the system prompt, built by distillation then RL; the toggle idea that hybrid models generalized.

title: GLM-4.5: agentic, reasoning, and coding (ARC) foundation models
why: A 355B/32B-active hybrid reasoning model with RL on multi-turn tool use; AIME 2024 91.0, SWE-bench Verified 64.2. Agentic RL in an open report.

title: Kimi K2: open agentic intelligence
why: A 1T/32B-active model trained with MuonClip on 15.5T tokens and large-scale agentic data synthesis; the base of K2 Thinking, which runs hundreds of sequential tool calls (slide 21).

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
why: QwQ emits 13 solutions and 901 tokens for 2+3; the first round is already correct over 92% of the time; a self-trained preference for efficient chains cuts MATH500 tokens by 48.6% at equal accuracy. Slide 20.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: Thoughts are all over the place: on the underthinking of o1-like LLMs
why: Wrong answers switch between lines of thought more often than right ones; a decoding penalty on switching (TIP) raises accuracy without retraining.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: L1: controlling how long a reasoning model thinks with reinforcement learning
why: Length-controlled policy optimization: a target length in the prompt, a reward for hitting it; a 1.5B model beats GPT-4o at equal chain length and budget forcing by up to 20 points absolute.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: ThinkPrune: pruning long chain-of-thought of LLMs via reinforcement learning
why: Iteratively tighten the token limit during RL: R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B halves its AIME chain length for a 2-point drop.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: Reasoning models can be effective without thinking
why: Prefill an empty thinking block: at a 700-token budget NoThinking scores 51.3 against 28.9 for thinking on ACM 23, and with parallel samples it matches thinking at up to 9x lower latency.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: AdaptThink: reasoning models can learn when to think
why: RL that chooses between thinking and not thinking per problem: 53% shorter outputs and +2.4% accuracy on math.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: Thinkless: LLM learns when to think
why: A decoupled GRPO objective learns a <short>/<think> control token; long-chain use drops 50-90% on easy sets.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: The danger of overthinking: examining the reasoning-action dilemma in agentic tasks
why: 4,018 SWE-bench Verified trajectories: agents that deliberate instead of acting fail more; selecting low-overthinking runs gains about 30% at 43% lower cost. Slide 20's agent bullet.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: The Markovian Thinker: architecture-agnostic linear scaling of reasoning
why: Reason in fixed-size chunks with a carried state so compute is linear in chain length; 96K-token thinking at a fraction of the GPU-months. A response to the length-generalization problem.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: Stop overthinking: a survey on efficient reasoning for large language models
why: Model-, output- and prompt-based methods for shorter chains, catalogued; the reference list for slide 20.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: Thinking vs. doing: agents that reason by scaling test-time interaction
why: Scale the number of environment interactions rather than the chain: a curriculum over interaction length gives Gemma 3 12B state-of-the-art open web-agent results.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: Parallel-R1: towards parallel thinking via reinforcement learning
why: RL that rewards spawning and merging parallel sub-chains; +8.4% over sequential RL. Parallel thinking as a trained behavior, slide 21.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: Scaling over scaling: exploring test-time scaling plateau in large reasoning models
why: A saturation bound (TTSPM) for parallel and sequential test-time scaling; where the curve on slide 19 stops.

section_name: Inference: budgets, length control, parallel compute, tools, serving
title: CRITIC: large language models can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
why: Self-correction grounded in tool outputs (search, interpreters) rather than the model's own judgment; the precursor to tools inside the chain.

title: Reasoning models guide: reasoning effort, encrypted reasoning items, billing (developer documentation)
why: The effort levels, encrypted reasoning items and the billing of reasoning tokens as output; the GPT-6 Astra and GPT-5.6 entries on slide 23 come from the model and pricing pages linked here. Secondary source, read October 2026.

title: Thinking: adaptive thinking, effort, display and signed thinking blocks (developer documentation)
why: Effort levels, the deprecated budget_tokens parameter, summarized or omitted display, and signed thinking blocks that must be passed back across tool calls; the Claude rows on slide 23. Secondary source, read October 2026.

title: Gemini thinking: thinking levels, thought signatures, Deep Think (developer documentation)
why: thinking_level, thought signatures that carry reasoning across calls, and the retirement of the 2025 thinkingBudget parameter; the Gemini row on slide 23. Secondary source, read October 2026.

title: DeepSeek V4 model card and API documentation
why: Non-thinking, thinking-high and thinking-max modes for the 1.6T mixture-of-experts V4-Pro with 49B active parameters; a previous turn's reasoning_content is ignored in plain chat but must be passed back across tool calls. Secondary source, read October 2026.

title: Qwen3.8 model cards (Hugging Face)
why: Effort levels xhigh/medium/low with thinking that cannot be disabled, preserve-thinking on by default, and the revenue-gated license of the 2.4T model; slide 23. Secondary source, read October 2026.

title: Kimi K3 model card (Hugging Face)
why: 2.8T parameters with 104B active, effort levels low/high/max with thinking always on, and the Kimi K3 license; the training recipe (nine specialists, three domains by three effort levels, merged by on-policy distillation with a -1 reward for overshooting the budget) is in the technical report, arXiv:2607.24653; slides 23-24. Secondary source, read October 2026.

title: OpenAI's result at the 2025 ICPC World Finals (X thread, September 17, 2025)
why: 12 of 12 problems solved under contest rules: GPT-5 solved 11 on the first try and an experimental model the hardest on its ninth submission. OpenAI published no blog post; the thread is the primary statement, with Google DeepMind's blog covering Gemini 2.5 Deep Think's 10 of 12. Secondary source.

title: Advanced version of Gemini with Deep Think officially achieves gold-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad (blog, July 21, 2025)
why: 35 of 42 in natural language within the 4.5-hour limit, graded by IMO coordinators; the parallel-thinking Deep Think mode. The 2025 IMO row on slide 25. Secondary source.

title: MathArena: evaluating LLMs on uncontaminated math competitions
why: Evaluate on competitions as they happen: strong signs of contamination on AIME 2024, proof-writing below 40% on IMO 2025 at the time; the live leaderboard behind slide 25's saturation claims.

title: ARC-AGI-2: a new challenge for frontier AI reasoning systems
why: Every task solved by at least two humans in testing; o3-medium at 3.0% at launch; cost per task reported beside accuracy. The benchmark that put cost on the axis.

title: Humanity's Last Exam
why: 2,500 expert questions from about 1,000 contributors; o1 at 8.8% and R1 at 8.6% in January 2025 with calibration errors of 81-93%; the column on slide 23.

title: TinyZero: reproduce DeepSeek R1-Zero's countdown and multiplication tasks for under $30 (GitHub, January 2025)
why: A 3B Qwen base learns search and self-verification on the countdown game with plain RL in veRL; the $30 figure on slide 24. Secondary source.

title: verl: volcano engine reinforcement learning for LLMs (GitHub)
why: The most used open RL stack for reasoning models (GRPO, DAPO, PPO; vLLM and SGLang rollouts; FSDP and Megatron training); where DAPO, ReTool and most 2025-26 reproductions ran. Secondary source.

title: GSM-Symbolic: understanding the limitations of mathematical reasoning in large language models
why: Templated variants of GSM8K: scores fall and scatter when names and numbers change; one irrelevant clause (GSM-NoOp) drops accuracy by up to 65%. Slide 26.

title: A careful examination of large language model performance on grade school arithmetic
why: GSM1k, fresh problems matched to GSM8K: drops of up to 8% for some model families and none for others; contamination measured directly.

title: The illusion of thinking: understanding the strengths and limitations of reasoning models via the lens of problem complexity
why: Controllable puzzles show three regimes and a collapse beyond a complexity threshold, with effort falling as problems get harder. Read with the reply below.

title: Comment on 'The illusion of thinking: understanding the strengths and limitations of reasoning models via the lens of problem complexity'
why: The Hanoi collapse coincides with output-token limits, river crossing with n>5 is unsolvable as posed, and asking for a generating function instead of the move list succeeds. The harness, not only the model.

title: Measuring mathematical problem solving with the MATH dataset
why: 12,500 competition problems with step-by-step solutions; the benchmark every reasoning model saturated by 2025.

title: GPQA: a graduate-level Google-proof Q&A benchmark
why: 448 questions where PhD experts score 65% and skilled non-experts 34% with web access; GPT-4 scored 39% at launch and frontier models sit in the nineties by 2026. The GPQA column on slide 23.

title: FrontierMath: a benchmark for evaluating advanced mathematical reasoning in AI
why: Research-level problems with automatically checkable answers; under 2% at launch. One of the few math benchmarks with headroom in 2026.

title: LiveCodeBench: holistic and contamination free evaluation of large language models for code
why: Problems collected continuously from contests with release dates, so contamination can be measured by date window; the code analogue of MathArena.

title: Introducing SWE-bench Verified (blog, August 13, 2024)
why: 500 human-validated tasks from SWE-bench after 93 developers screened 1,699; GPT-4o from 16% on the original to 33.2%. The agentic benchmark quoted on slides 12 and 21. Secondary source.

title: Reasoning models better express their confidence
why: Reasoning models are better calibrated in 33 of 36 settings, traced to slow-thinking behaviors such as exploring alternatives and backtracking; slide 26.

title: Reasoning about uncertainty: do reasoning models know when they don't know?
why: Stated confidence often above 85% on wrong answers, with longer chains more overconfident; introspection helps some models and hurts others. The other half of slide 26.

title: Thinking out loud: do reasoning models know when they're right?
why: Reasoning models verbalize confidence better but abstain less, saying 'I don't know' at lower rates: a reasoning tax on honesty.

title: Monitoring reasoning models for misbehavior and the risks of promoting obfuscation
why: A GPT-4o monitor reading o3-mini's chain catches reward hacking in agentic coding with 95% recall against 60% from actions alone; training against the monitor hides the hacking (recall near zero) without stopping it. The monitorability tax, slide 27.

title: Chain of thought monitorability: a new and fragile opportunity for AI safety
why: A 41-author position paper across labs: chains of thought are monitorable today for reasons that may not last; keep them legible and report monitorability in model cards.

title: Monitoring monitorability
why: Thirteen evaluations in 24 environments: current models 'fairly, but not perfectly, monitorable'; longer chains more monitorable; RL at current scale did not materially degrade monitorability in two runs.

title: OpenAI o3 and o4-mini system card (April 2025)
why: PersonQA hallucination rates of 33% (o3) and 48% (o4-mini) against 16% for o1, as reported in the card and widely covered; the slide-26 tile. Secondary source.

title: Reasoning models struggle to control their chains of thought, and that's good (research post, March 5, 2026)
why: Models asked to steer their own chain content succeed between 0.1% and 15.4% of the time at baseline, and the rate falls with further RL training; slide 27. Secondary source.

title: GPT-6 Astra system card (September 3, 2026)
why: Reports chain-of-thought monitorability below earlier models and evaluation awareness in 9.6% of chains against 2.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol in a Codex deployment simulation, and says the authors take the trend seriously; slide 27. Secondary source.

title: A survey of reasoning with foundation models
why: The pre-o1 map of reasoning methods, useful for seeing which 2023 ideas survived RL (verifiers, tools, search) and which did not (prompt-time graph search).

title: Towards concise and adaptive thinking in large reasoning models: a survey
why: Methods for shorter and adaptive chains, organized by where the control sits; complements Sui et al. for the slide-29 'using' column.

title: The state of LLM reasoning models (newsletter, March 2025)
why: A roundup of inference-time scaling methods published after R1, grouped by what they change; a practitioner's checklist. Secondary source.

title: Test-time scaling in reasoning LLMs: inference regimes, evaluation, and reproducibility
why: A 2026 taxonomy of test-time scaling (sequential, leaf, prefix) with 1.4M released attempts; the evaluation protocol slide 29 asks for, spelled out.

title: Introducing GPT-5 (blog, August 7, 2025)
why: The first frontier release with a router choosing when to think and a claim of about six times fewer factual errors than o3 in thinking mode; the hybrid default that 2026 models made universal. Secondary source.

authors: Gibney (Scientific American, reprinted from Nature news)
title: Secrets of DeepSeek AI model revealed in landmark paper (September 17, 2025)
why: The peer-reviewed R1 paper's supplement puts the RL phase at about $294,000 on H800s (at an assumed $2 per GPU-hour) on top of a roughly $6M base model; the figure quoted on slides 12 and 24. Secondary source.
